# Brown & Brown (NYSE:BRO) - Senior Vice President, IT Strategy & Innovation briefing packet
| Senior Vice President, IT Strategy & Innovation | Not provided | Reports to CITO (enterprise technology strategy) |

## JD Complement
The role sits at the intersection of a large, acquisition-driven insurance intermediary and a modern enterprise technology agenda. The operating tension is not “build a product,” but “standardize enough to scale while preserving the local,
producer-led model that drives growth.”

Brown & Brown’s context implies this leader must translate a decentralized business into a more interoperable technology estate without slowing the pace of acquisitions, teammate productivity, or client service.

## Company DNA & Operating Model
Brown & Brown is a regulated insurance brokerage and risk intermediary, not a software company. It wins through distribution, relationships, specialty expertise, and disciplined M&A, with growth amplified by a long-running producer-led
culture.

The archetype is hybrid: services-led with strong partner/channel economics and a platform-like need for shared data, workflow, and governance across many businesses. The central tension is local autonomy versus enterprise consistency.

The company’s culture language emphasizes meritocracy and self-starters, which usually means influence is earned through execution, not central mandate. For technology, that often creates a need for pragmatic standards, not heavy-handed
transformation theater.

## Company Strategy & Operating Pressure
Brown & Brown was founded in 1939 and has grown into one of the largest insurance brokerages in the world, with over 23,000 teammates worldwide. It is publicly traded on the NYSE under BRO and operates under the scrutiny of investors who
expect durable organic growth plus acquisition integration.

A major strategic pressure is scale management: every acquisition adds books of business, systems, data, and operating variation. The technology strategy role likely exists to reduce integration friction, improve decision rights, and make
enterprise capabilities reusable across a growing footprint.

The company’s recent acquisition activity, including the announced agreement to acquire Accession Risk Management Group in 2025, reinforces the need for architecture that can absorb growth without creating a brittle core.
